query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-depositing an ultra‐thin, conformal copper coating on tungsten particles (via an atomic layer deposition process) prior to consolidation will eliminate interfacial voids and phase separation, resulting in a W–Cu composite with significantly improved thermal transport while preserving good mechanical durability relative to conventional infiltration or sintering processes.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W regions embedded in a Cu matrix that show phase separation or void formation during conventional consolidation processing.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, conformal copper coating on the tungsten surfaces using atomic layer deposition (ALD) before the composite consolidation process (e.g., spark-plasma sintering).
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled temperatures below the copper boiling point and in an inert or reducing atmosphere to prevent oxidation; subsequent sintering/assembly to simulate service conditions in fusion-reactor joints under irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform, nanoscale Cu interlayer at the W–Cu interfaces that promotes intimate metallurgical bonding.
generation.mechanism: The ALD copper layer enhances wettability and interdiffusion during sintering, thereby reducing the formation of voids and minimizing phase separation at the W–Cu interfaces. This improved interface reduces thermal resistance while maintaining the mechanical integrity of the composite under thermal and irradiation stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ALD-treated composite will show enhanced thermal conductivity due to nearly perfect interfacial contact, reduced void content, and maintained or improved mechanical durability compared to composites produced by conventional infiltration or sintering methods.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication methods where tungsten particles are directly infiltrated with molten or sintered copper (via spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying) that typically yield voids and phase separation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to work under processing conditions that avoid excessive temperatures that might induce copper boiling or uncontrolled diffusion, and within the service environment typical for fusion-reactor heat-transfer joints (i.e., high thermal flux and irradiation exposure).
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the scalability of the ALD process to uniformly coat complex W geometries and the long-term adhesion stability of the deposited Cu layer under cyclic thermal and irradiation conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with tungsten particles pre-coated with Cu via ALD and a control set fabricated using conventional methods (e.g., direct Cu infiltration or SPS without pre-coating). Subject both sets to identical sintering schedules followed by accelerated thermal cycling and simulated irradiation in a controlled reactor environment.
measurements: Measure the interfacial void density and phase homogeneity using high-resolution electron microscopy.
Determine thermal conductivity across the composite using laser flash analysis.
Assess mechanical durability via tensile and compression tests before and after thermal/irradiation exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated composites do not show a statistically significant reduction in interfacial voids and an improvement in thermal conductivity (and/or mechanical properties) compared to the conventional composites under the identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that the ALD pre-coating intervention overcomes fabrication limitations is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. Furthermore, blistering at moderate temperature (<800 K) by D and He ( [2] , [3] ) and the formation of pits, holes, and bubbles by He at higher temperature (>1600 K) ( [4] ) have all been observed.
